**Proof.**

Let

$$G = \pi_1(\Sigma_g) \cong \bigl\langle x_1, y_1, \dots, x_g, y_g \;\big|\; [x_1, y_1]\cdots[x_g, y_g] \bigr\rangle,$$

and let $F_g = \langle a_1, \dots, a_g \rangle$ be the free group on $g$ generators.

We define a map on the generators of $G$ by

$$\varphi(x_i) = a_i, \qquad \varphi(y_i) = 1 \quad (i = 1, \dots, g).$$

By the universal property of free groups, this extends uniquely to a homomorphism $\widetilde{\varphi} : \langle x_1, y_1, \dots, x_g, y_g \rangle \to F_g$ from the free group on the $2g$ generators $\{x_i, y_i\}$ onto $F_g$.

To show that $\widetilde{\varphi}$ descends to a well-defined homomorphism $\varphi : G \to F_g$, we must verify that the single defining relator of $G$ lies in $\ker \widetilde{\varphi}$. The relator is $[x_1, y_1]\cdots[x_g, y_g]$. For each $i$,

$$\widetilde{\varphi}\bigl([x_i, y_i]\bigr) = \bigl[\widetilde{\varphi}(x_i),\, \widetilde{\varphi}(y_i)\bigr] = [a_i, 1] = 1,$$

since the commutator of any element with the identity is the identity. Therefore

$$\widetilde{\varphi}\bigl([x_1, y_1]\cdots[x_g, y_g]\bigr) = \prod_{i=1}^{g} \widetilde{\varphi}\bigl([x_i, y_i]\bigr) = \prod_{i=1}^{g} 1 = 1.$$

Hence the relator is sent to the identity, so $\widetilde{\varphi}$ factors through the quotient and yields a well-defined homomorphism

$$\varphi : G \longrightarrow F_g.$$

It remains to show that $\varphi$ is surjective. Each free generator $a_i$ of $F_g$ is the image of $x_i \in G$:

$$\varphi(x_i) = a_i, \qquad i = 1, \dots, g.$$

Since the images of the $x_i$ generate $F_g$, the homomorphism $\varphi$ is surjective.

Thus $\varphi : \pi_1(\Sigma_g) \to F_g$ is an epimorphism, constructed purely algebraically from the given presentation. $\blacksquare$

### PROOF COMPLETE
